title: Microsoft Power Platform Solution Architect Expert (PL-600)

nodes.title: Microsoft Dataverse: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Dataverse is the data platform underneath the Power Platform — a managed, relational store with built-in security, business logic, and a uniform Web API. PL-400 leans on it heavily: most Power Apps, plug-ins, and automations read and write Dataverse.

flashcards.front: What is a Dataverse table (formerly entity)?
flashcards.back: A table is a typed set of rows with columns, relationships, keys, and its own security. Standard tables (Account, Contact) ship with the platform; custom tables are added per solution. Each table exposes an OData/Web API endpoint automatically.

flashcards.front: How do you query Dataverse from code?
flashcards.back: Use the Web API — an OData v4 REST endpoint at /api/data/v9.x. GET with $select/$filter/$expand for reads, POST/PATCH/DELETE for writes. The SDK (IOrganizationService) wraps the same operations for plug-ins and server-side code.

flashcards.front: How is access controlled in Dataverse?
flashcards.back: Security roles grant privileges (create/read/write/delete/append) at access levels (user, business unit, parent-child, organization). Rows are owned by a user or team; business units scope visibility. This is row- and column-level security, not just table-level.

flashcards.front: Business rules vs plug-ins for logic?
flashcards.back: Business rules are no-code, run on the form and server for simple validation/defaults. Plug-ins are .NET code on the event pipeline for complex or cross-table logic. Prefer the lightest tool that meets the requirement — business rules first, plug-ins when you need real code.

questions.q: A solution architect is gathering requirements for a Power Platform engagement. The customer wants every functional requirement traced back to a measurable business outcome before any build work starts. Which artifact is the most appropriate to produce in this phase?
choices: An Application Lifecycle Management (ALM) pipeline definition in Azure DevOps
A managed solution exported from the developer environment for review
A Dataverse environment strategy listing dev, test and production environments
A solution blueprint that maps stakeholder objectives, KPIs and functional requirements
questions.explanation: Solution envisioning artifacts — typically a blueprint or vision document — capture stakeholder objectives, success measures (KPIs) and the functional requirements that flow from them, and they live in the envisioning phase before any build occurs. An ALM pipeline is a delivery artifact produced during implementation, not envisioning, and assumes the design already exists. The environment strategy is part of architecting the solution, not gathering requirements; it answers 'where will it run', not 'what business outcome are we delivering'. Exporting a managed solution is a build/release activity — there is nothing to export yet at the envisioning stage.

questions.q: Your customer must store 600 GB of relational business data with row-level security, complex relationships and built-in auditing. The team also wants the same data surfaced in a model-driven app and in Power BI. Which storage option should the architect recommend?
choices: SharePoint Online lists with column formatting for the model-driven app
Azure Blob Storage with a custom connector exposed to Power Apps
Microsoft Dataverse as the primary data store
Azure Table Storage referenced through a virtual table
questions.explanation: Dataverse is purpose-built for Power Platform workloads: it scales well past hundreds of GB, supports complex relationships, role-based and row-level security, native auditing, and is the only data source that fully powers model-driven apps. SharePoint lists are capped at limits unsuitable for 600 GB of relational data and cannot host model-driven apps. Azure Blob Storage is for unstructured files and has no concept of rows, relationships or row-level security. Azure Table Storage exposed as a virtual table can surface in canvas apps, but it is a NoSQL key/value store — it lacks the relational modelling, auditing and model-driven app support the requirements call for.

questions.q: A regulated customer wants their Power Platform deployment isolated from other tenants for the production workload, with restricted maker access and strict DLP. They also need developer sandboxes that don't count against production licensing. Which environment strategy fits best?
choices: Use a single default environment for all makers and deploy directly to production
Provision a managed production environment plus developer-type environments for each maker
Use one production environment and grant every maker the Environment Maker role in production
Create only Trial environments per project so unused ones expire automatically
questions.explanation: The recommended pattern is a managed production environment (where you can apply DLP, security groups, sharing limits and other Power Platform admin governance controls) combined with per-maker developer-type environments (free of charge, single-user, ideal for build/experiment). The default environment is shared by every user in the tenant and cannot be isolated, so it is unsuitable for a regulated workload. Granting Environment Maker in production lets makers build directly in production — the opposite of the requested isolation and governance posture. Trial environments expire after 30 days and are not designed as developer sandboxes, so relying on them for ongoing development is operationally fragile.

questions.q: The customer's ALM strategy must move Power Apps, Power Automate flows and Dataverse customizations from dev to test to production with no manual rebuilding, while honouring environment-specific values such as connection references and SharePoint site URLs. Which approach should the solution architect endorse?
choices: Export and import unmanaged solutions between environments and edit values by hand after each import
Use the 'Save as' feature in the maker portal to clone each app per environment
Share each app and flow individually via run-only users to recreate them in each environment
Use managed solutions with environment variables and deployment settings files in a pipeline
questions.explanation: Managed solutions are Microsoft's recommended deployment unit for non-development environments, and environment variables (combined with deployment settings files used by Power Platform CLI or Power Platform Build Tools pipelines) are designed precisely so values like connection references, SharePoint URLs and API endpoints differ per target environment without code changes. Unmanaged solutions allow makers to edit components directly in production, which breaks ALM hygiene, and hand-editing values per environment is error-prone. Sharing apps via run-only users does not deploy the artifacts to another environment at all — it just grants runtime access where they already exist. 'Save as' clones an app within the same environment and creates an orphaned copy, not a controlled deployment.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.
Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.
Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

questions.q: A model-driven app must restrict salespeople so that each user only sees the Account records they own and the Accounts owned by their direct reports — never Accounts owned by other business units. Which Dataverse security construct delivers this without per-record sharing?
choices: Field-level security profiles applied to the Account table
A team-owned record assignment with a single global team
A security role that grants User-level read on Account, combined with the manager hierarchy security
A Power Automate flow that filters records before the app renders them
questions.explanation: Dataverse hierarchy security (configured on the manager hierarchy) layered on top of a security role with User-level (basic) read access on Account gives a user visibility to their own records plus those owned by users who report to them, exactly matching the requirement. Field-level security profiles control which columns a user can see — not which rows — so they cannot answer 'which Accounts'. Assigning every record to a single global team gives every team member identical access to every record, the opposite of the requirement. A Power Automate flow filtering records is not a security boundary: users can still query the data through the API, advanced find or another app, so it leaks data.

questions.q: A customer needs to surface real-time SAP ERP data inside a Dataverse-driven model-driven app without copying the data into Dataverse and without writing custom plug-in code. Which integration pattern best fits?
choices: Use Dataverse virtual tables backed by an OData or custom connector provider
Schedule a nightly Power Automate flow that imports SAP rows into a Dataverse table
Embed a Power BI report that queries SAP via DirectQuery into every form
Write a custom plug-in that synchronously calls SAP on every record read
questions.explanation: Virtual tables let Dataverse surface external data as if it were a native table — read (and optionally write) operations are proxied to the source system at query time — and an OData or custom connector provider is the standard way to expose SAP through one. A nightly import copies the data, which violates the no-copy and real-time requirements. Embedding a DirectQuery Power BI report shows the data in a visual but does not expose it as a Dataverse table that can drive views, business rules or workflows, so it does not satisfy the 'inside a Dataverse-driven model-driven app' requirement. Writing a plug-in that calls SAP on every record read introduces synchronous external calls into the platform pipeline — Microsoft explicitly warns against this and the virtual table provider exists precisely to avoid that pattern.

questions.q: A custom Dataverse plug-in must call a downstream API that occasionally takes longer than 2 minutes to respond. The architect needs to keep the plug-in within the platform's sandbox limits and avoid blocking the user's save. What is the recommended pattern?
choices: Register the plug-in synchronously in the PostOperation stage so the user waits for completion
Move the long-running work to an Azure Function or Logic App, invoked from the plug-in via a service-bus or HTTP message
Increase the plug-in sandbox CPU and timeout quotas through the Power Platform admin center
Loop with Thread.Sleep inside the plug-in until the API responds
questions.explanation: Dataverse sandbox plug-ins have a hard 2-minute execution limit; for longer-running work, Microsoft recommends offloading to an Azure Function or Logic App and invoking it from the plug-in via Azure Service Bus (preferred for guaranteed delivery) or an asynchronous HTTP request. A synchronous PostOperation plug-in still has to finish inside the 2-minute window and blocks the user the entire time. The sandbox CPU and timeout quotas are platform-set and cannot be raised through the admin center. Thread.Sleep wastes the sandbox CPU budget, still risks the 2-minute timeout and is explicitly listed by Microsoft as an anti-pattern in plug-in code.

questions.q: A Power Platform solution will reuse a corporate Azure AD application registration to call the Microsoft Graph from inside a canvas app. Sign-in must use the end user's identity, not a service principal. Which connector / authentication pattern should the architect choose?
choices: A custom connector configured with OAuth 2.0 (Authorization Code) against the Azure AD app
A custom connector with API key authentication, sharing one key across all users
An on-premises data gateway with Windows authentication mapped to the Azure AD app
A Power Automate flow using the HTTP action with a hard-coded client secret
questions.explanation: A custom connector using OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code against the existing Azure AD app registration produces a delegated token for the signed-in user, so the Microsoft Graph call runs in that user's identity context with their consent and permissions. API key authentication shares a single static secret across every user, which is neither user-context auth nor an acceptable secret-management practice. The on-premises data gateway brokers on-prem traffic and Windows authentication; it is not the mechanism for an Azure AD delegated flow to a cloud API. An HTTP action with a hard-coded client secret performs an application-only client-credentials call (service principal), which is the exact pattern the requirement excludes, and it also hard-codes a secret outside any secure store.

nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

questions.q: An enterprise wants to allow makers to build apps with most connectors but block any flow or app that mixes Microsoft 365 / Dataverse data with public social-media connectors in the same resource. Which Power Platform governance feature should the architect configure?
choices: Solution checker rules enforced in the maker portal
Conditional access policies in Microsoft Entra ID scoped to Power Apps
A Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policy classifying connectors as Business / Non-Business / Blocked
Customer-managed keys (CMK) on the Dataverse environment
questions.explanation: Power Platform Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies classify connectors into Business, Non-Business and Blocked groups, and prevent apps or flows from combining connectors from different groups in the same resource — which is precisely the scenario described. Solution checker runs static analysis for code quality and basic security findings; it does not enforce connector data-grouping rules at runtime. Conditional Access policies control sign-in conditions to Power Apps (device, location, MFA) but do not understand connector groupings within a flow. Customer-managed keys encrypt Dataverse data at rest using a key from Azure Key Vault — that controls encryption, not which connectors a maker can combine.

questions.q: A model-driven app already exists for the sales team in Dataverse. The customer wants to add an external partner portal where unauthenticated visitors can submit a lead, and authenticated partners can view their own related cases — all using the same Dataverse tables. Which Power Platform product fits?
choices: A Power Apps canvas app shared with the external partner organization
A Power Pages site bound to the Dataverse environment with web roles and table permissions
A SharePoint communication site fronted with a Power Automate intake form
A Power BI workspace shared with external Azure AD B2B guests
questions.explanation: Power Pages is the Power Platform product for public, low-code external-facing websites that read and write the same Dataverse tables an internal app uses; it supports anonymous visitors, multiple identity providers (B2C / Azure AD / local accounts) and fine-grained access through web roles plus table permissions. Sharing a canvas app with external users still requires per-user Power Apps licensing and an internal sign-in — it is not a public anonymous portal. A SharePoint site with a Power Automate intake form is not bound to Dataverse rows in a record-by-record way and does not surface 'each partner's own cases' securely. A Power BI workspace is read-only reporting and cannot accept anonymous lead submissions, so it solves neither half of the requirement.

questions.q: An architect must propose a disaster-recovery target for a Dataverse production environment. The customer has accepted up to 24 hours of data loss but cannot tolerate restoring to a brand-new URL because integrations are hard-wired to the existing environment URL. Which capability should be highlighted in the design?
choices: Long-term retention by exporting Dataverse tables to Azure Data Lake daily
A copy of production into a sandbox environment for the integration team to repoint to
Customer-managed keys with key vault soft-delete enabled
System-generated daily backups restored into the same environment via the Power Platform admin center
questions.explanation: Dataverse system-generated backups are retained for up to 28 days (longer for production-type environments with appropriate licensing) and can be restored over the same production environment in place, preserving the existing URL — which directly satisfies the integration constraint. Restoring into a sandbox copy creates a different environment URL and forces every integration to be repointed, the exact thing the customer wants to avoid. Customer-managed keys with soft-delete protect the encryption key from accidental deletion but do not by themselves recover deleted or corrupted data, so they are not a DR mechanism. Daily exports to a data lake give you an analytics archive, not an in-place transactional restore of Dataverse — recreating the live system from a lake export is neither supported nor timely.

questions.q: During testing, a model-driven app loads slowly because a custom JavaScript form script runs a synchronous Web API call on every form load. The architect must recommend a fix that follows Microsoft's performance guidance. What should be done?
choices: Replace the synchronous call with an asynchronous Web API call using Promises, and defer non-critical work to form-load events that fire after the form is rendered
Move the JavaScript into a plug-in registered on the Retrieve message so it runs server-side instead
Cache the response in localStorage for 30 days so future loads skip the call entirely
Convert the model-driven app form into a canvas app embedded in the same record
questions.explanation: Microsoft's documented form-script performance guidance is to avoid synchronous Web API calls in form scripts because they block the UI thread; the recommended fix is asynchronous calls (Promises / async-await), with non-critical work deferred to later form events so the initial render is not blocked. Moving the logic to a Retrieve plug-in adds latency to every record read across every client, including views and APIs, and is a documented anti-pattern. Caching dynamic record data in localStorage for 30 days produces stale data with no invalidation strategy and can leak data on shared machines. Swapping the form for an embedded canvas app is a costly architectural rewrite that does not address the underlying synchronous-call anti-pattern.
